design_df.definition: J + r - k, where J is units, k the number of fixed-effects columns, restricted to the rows of the assignment, that the sequential rule (ir.md, Sequential rule for aliased columns) keeps on these rows and r their within-level rank. Q holds the k kept columns, each divided by its largest absolute value and made orthonormal in column order by two passes of Gram-Schmidt over the rows, each column in turn losing twice its projection onto the columns of Q before it and being then divided by its norm. Q_d is Q with the first row of each level of the unit, in table order, subtracted from every row of the level. r is the number of columns of Q_d that the sequential rule keeps when it compares the norm of each residual, in the units of Q_d, with 1e-7, its tolerance, times the norm of the same column of Q, which is 1, in place of the norm of the column of Q_d. A combination of the columns is constant within the levels exactly when the subtraction maps it to 0, so in exact arithmetic r is the rank of the columns centred within the levels, and design_df equals the number of indicator columns of the levels that the sequential rule keeps when it is applied to the fixed-effects columns followed by the indicator columns, without building the n by J indicator matrix. Each column of Q has lost what the columns before it explain, such as a constant added to it when the intercept comes first, so that r does not change with such a constant, and differences within the levels that come from rounding stay near the rounding error of a unit vector and are not counted, as the indicator columns would absorb them. It gives back units, so it takes the count class of units.

df.definition: The number of columns of this term that the sequential rule keeps when it is applied to a column of ones, whether or not the fixed part has an intercept, followed by the columns of the main-effect terms in column order. These kept columns, without the column of ones, are the columns of gvif.

gvif.definition: det(R_TT) det(R_OO) / det(R), where R is the matrix of Pearson correlations, over the rows of the design sample, between the kept columns of the main-effect terms, T are the kept columns of this term, O the other kept columns and the determinant of an empty matrix is 1. It is computed as the product over the columns j of T of (a_j / b_j)^2, which equals the ratio of determinants: the columns are divided by their largest absolute values, so that no sum or product of their values overflows or underflows, centred, with means summed exactly and divided once as ir.md (Centring) computes means, and scaled to unit Euclidean length, b_j is the norm of the residual of column j after orthogonal projection onto the columns of O and the earlier columns of T, in that order, and a_j the norm of its residual after projection onto the earlier columns of T alone, each computed as the sequential rule computes residuals (ir.md). Its relative error grows with its value, as for any method, so the two packages compare it within a tolerance that grows with it (conventions.md, Comparison across languages).

gvif_per_df.definition: gvif raised to the power 1/df, which equals the variance inflation factor for a term with one column. It is compared within the same tolerance as gvif.

entries.summary: Computes the generalised variance inflation factor of each main-effect term from the fixed-effects matrix, which does not change with the coding of a factor's contrasts. Interaction terms are left out, because the factor of a lower-order term in a model with its interactions depends on the centring of the variables it interacts with. The check reads the design only and ignores the covariance of the fitted model, so it describes the design rather than the standard errors of a fit.

high.rationale: The upper value of the same rule of thumb.

sources.citation: James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2013). An introduction to statistical learning: With applications in R. Springer.

moderate.rationale: A widely quoted rule of thumb treats a variance inflation factor above 5 or 10 as a problematic amount of collinearity. Comparing the factor per degree of freedom with it extends the rule to terms with several columns, an extension of this project that the sources do not state.

sources.citation: James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2013). An introduction to statistical learning: With applications in R. Springer.
Fox, J., & Monette, G. (1992). Generalized collinearity diagnostics. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 87(417), 178-183.

Fox and Monette (1992) define the generalised variance inflation factor and the dimension-adjusted GVIF^(1/(2 df)), which car's documentation describes as comparable across terms of different dimension. Comparing GVIF^(1/df) with 5 and 10 is the same as comparing GVIF^(1/(2 df)) with the square roots of 5 and 10, about 2.24 and 3.16, which reduces to the rule of thumb for a term with one column.

condition_number.definition: The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value of the matrix of the fixed-effects columns that the sequential rule keeps, the intercept included, each divided by its largest absolute value and then scaled to unit Euclidean length. The singular values are those of that matrix itself, computed by a backward-stable singular value decomposition such as LAPACK's, through svd() in R and numpy.linalg.svd in Python, never the square roots of the eigenvalues of its cross-product, whose error grows with the square of the condition number. The relative error of the smallest singular value then grows with the condition number, so the two packages compare it within a tolerance that grows with its value (conventions.md, Comparison across languages).

scaled_columns.definition: The fixed-effects columns, other than the intercept, that the sequential rule keeps, that belong to terms whose variables are all numeric and that take a value other than 0 and 1 in the design sample, in column order.

sd_largest.definition: The largest standard deviation of those columns, with denominator n - 1, where n is the number of rows of the design sample. The standard deviation of a column whose values are all equal, compared by value, is 0. That of any other column is M times the standard deviation of the column divided by its largest absolute value M, which keeps the squares from overflowing or underflowing, computed from its mean, summed exactly and divided once as ir.md (Centring) computes means, as the square root of the sum of the squared differences from the mean, divided by n - 1.

sd_ratio.definition: sd_largest divided by sd_smallest, absent when sd_smallest is 0.

sd_smallest.definition: The smallest of those standard deviations.

entries.summary: Anticipates lme4's warning that predictors are on very different scales, which it gives with the default settings of lmerControl() when the standard deviations of the fixed-effects columns that it keeps and that are not all 0 or 1 differ by a factor above 1000, or when one of them lies above 1000 or below 0.001. The warning concerns the units of the columns, so the check also reports the condition number of the fixed-effects matrix with columns scaled to unit length, which measures near-dependence between the columns and which a change of units does not alter. Columns coded from categorical predictors are left out of the standard deviations, because their contrasts lie between -1 and 1, so that they rarely set off the warning, and because their standard deviations give back the counts of the levels.

budget.definition: J - k + r, where J is levels, k the number of fixed-effects columns that the sequential rule keeps and r the within-level rank of those columns for the levels of the factor, computed as assignment.design_df states. In exact arithmetic it equals the number of indicator columns of the factor, one for each level, that the sequential rule keeps when it is applied to the fixed-effects columns followed by the indicator columns. It is a number of degrees of freedom, but it equals levels minus 1 when the intercept is the only fixed effect that is constant within levels, so it takes the count class of levels, so that it cannot give back a suppressed count of levels (docs/spec/privacy.md).

consuming_terms.definition: The fixed terms, the intercept included, in term order, whose kept columns lower the budget: a term t is listed when the budget computed as above from the kept fixed-effects columns of the terms up to and including t is below the budget computed from the terms before t, the budget of no terms being the number of levels. Gram-Schmidt and the sequential rule treat each column in turn, so one computation of the within-level rank gives every one of these budgets. The list is not empty when budget is below levels.

levels.definition: The number of levels of the factor in the design sample.

entries.summary: Counts the independent contrasts between the levels of a grouping factor that remain after the fixed effects, d = rank([X, Z]) - rank(X) with Z the indicator matrix of the factor. When it is 0, as when the factor is also a fixed effect or its levels are used up by level-constant covariates, the variance of its random intercept is not identified under REML. In balanced random-intercept designs it equals the denominator degrees of freedom for effects that are constant within levels. It is computed by rank, never by counting columns, because columns that vary within levels can combine into a direction that does not.

max_z_columns.definition: The largest number of columns of Z for which the check runs. With max_parameters, it bounds the time of the check, which grows with the square of the number of columns of Z times the square of the largest number of columns of a random term, and with the number of rows times the square of the number of random terms, which max_parameters bounds. The check holds W in blocks, the elements between a few of the levels of one random term and the columns of the terms after it at a time, so that its memory does not grow with the square of the number of columns of Z.

null_loading.definition: The share of the largest square root of a diagonal element of the projector at or above which a parameter belongs to the confounded set.

sources.citation: Set by this project for registry 0.1.0.

rank_tolerance.definition: The relative tolerance at or below which an eigenvalue of the scaled Gram matrix, or the ratio of a diagonal element of the Gram matrix to the same element of the unprojected basis, counts as zero. A finding is near_threshold when any eigenvalue of C, or any of these ratios, lies within the proximity factor of it (registry.md, Parameters).

sources.citation: Set by this project for registry 0.1.0. Exactly confounded parameters give eigenvalues at the level of rounding error, near 1e-16, far below it.

remedies.description: Remove or merge the random terms whose parameters are confounded, starting with those named, or change a coding that makes uncorrelated terms unidentified.

confounded_parameters.definition: The parameters k of C with sqrt(d_k) at least null_loading times the largest sqrt(d_j), where d_k is the sum of v_ik squared over an orthonormal basis v_1, ..., v_r of the eigenvectors of C whose eigenvalues are at or below rank_tolerance, the diagonal of the projector onto their span, named as the IR names them in their IR order. The projector does not depend on the basis chosen, so that every confounded parameter is named however the eigenvalues at rounding level are ordered. The list is empty when no eigenvalue is at or below rank_tolerance.

parameters.definition: The number of covariance parameters of the random terms, a variance for each column of a term and a covariance for each pair of columns of a term that estimates correlations, plus 1 for the residual variance when the family class is gaussian.

rank.definition: parameters minus the number of vanishing parameters minus the number of eigenvalues of C at or below rank_tolerance. For the gaussian family class, let X be the fixed-effects columns that the sequential rule keeps, P = I - X(X'X)^-1 X', Z the random-effects matrix of the IR on the design sample with each column of a random term, in every level, divided by its largest absolute value over the design sample unless it is 0 in every row, D the residual basis, which is I without weights and diag(m/w) for weights w with m the smallest weight, diag(1/w) divided by its largest element, and W = Z'PZ. For other family classes, W = Z'Z, and the residual and the weights are left out. The divisions keep the products below from overflowing or underflowing, and they change M to SMS for a diagonal matrix S with positive elements, which leaves C, the vanishing test and the verdict unchanged. Each covariance parameter k has a symmetric basis matrix A_k over the columns of Z: 1 at the diagonal position of the column in every level of the term's factor for a variance, and 1 at the two positions of the pair of columns in every level for a covariance. The Gram matrix M has M_kl = tr(A_k W A_l W) for covariance parameters, M_ks = tr(A_k Z'PDPZ) between a covariance parameter and the residual, and M_ss = tr(PDPD), which is n - rank(X) without weights, with n the number of rows of the design sample. A covariance parameter vanishes when M_kk is at or below rank_tolerance times tr(A_k Z'Z A_k Z'Z), the same element of its unprojected basis, and the residual when M_ss is at or below rank_tolerance times tr(DD), which is n without weights, so that the test does not depend on the units of the columns. C is M restricted to the other parameters and scaled to C_kl = M_kl / sqrt(M_kk M_ll). Its eigenvalues and eigenvectors are computed in one call of LAPACK's solver for symmetric matrices, through eigen(symmetric = TRUE) in R and numpy.linalg.eigh in Python, which differ only in rounding, and confounded_parameters takes its eigenvectors from the same call.

smallest_eigenvalue.definition: The smallest eigenvalue of C, a scale-free index of how close the design comes to confounding parameters. It is a heuristic, absent when C is empty, which the verdict does not read. It is computed from the level sizes of the factors and the rows of the design sample, so that for a random intercept beside a fixed part constant within its levels it gives back the rows and the level sizes that the privacy filter suppresses, and a shareable document never writes it.

vanishing_parameters.definition: The vanishing parameters, which the fixed effects absorb, named as the IR names them (ir.md, Covariance parameters) in their IR order.

verdict.definition: not_identified when rank is below parameters, and otherwise identified for the gaussian family class and necessary_condition_met for the other family classes, for which the test covers a necessary condition only.

entries.summary: Tests whether the covariance parameters of the random part can be separated by the design, before any fit. For a Gaussian model whose covariance parameters enter the marginal covariance linearly, the parameters are identified under REML if and only if their REML-projected covariance bases and the projection itself are linearly independent, which the rank of their Gram matrix decides. The rank of Z is the wrong criterion. For other family classes, the check uses the unprojected bases on the latent scale without the residual, which gives a necessary condition only, so the verdict is then necessary_condition_met rather than identified (02-decisions.md, Q3). The space spanned by the eigenvectors of the vanishing eigenvalues names the parameters that the design confounds.
entries.title: Identifiability of the covariance parameters

adequate.fallback: '{term}' has {dimension} for each level of '{factor}', and more levels than that vary in all its columns.
adequate.template: In {informative} of the {levels} of '{factor}', all columns of '{term}' vary, and the term has {dimension} for each level.

guaranteed.fallback: '{term}' has {dimension} for each level of '{factor}', more than its levels can support, so the fit will be singular. A fit reported as non-singular would suggest that the optimiser stopped early.
guaranteed.template: '{term}' has {dimension} for each level of '{factor}', but with {levels} the covariance matrix of these effects has rank {bound} at most, so the fit will be singular. A fit reported as non-singular would suggest that the optimiser stopped early.

likely.fallback: In few levels of '{factor}' do all columns of '{term}' vary, no more than its {dimension} for each level, so a singular fit is likely.
likely.template: In only {informative} of '{factor}' do all columns of '{term}' vary, no more than its {dimension} for each level, so a singular fit is likely.

references.citation: 02-decisions.md, Q3

Review catalogue (docs/design/evidence/review-catalogue.md), L1-07. The verifier gives the bound J - 1 when every column of the term, or at least its intercept, also appears in the fixed part, and reports rank 1 in 10 of 10 fits at J = 2 with a fixed intercept only. counterparts requires every column, which is stricter, because 'guaranteed' needs the proof that the case of every column gives and 10 simulated fits do not.

remedies.description: Reduce the term along the plan's ladder, removing correlations before variances and terms that few levels inform before the others.

bound.definition: levels minus 1 when counterparts is true, and levels otherwise. It gives back levels, so it takes the count class of levels.

counterparts.definition: Whether the sequential rule, applied to the fixed-effects columns followed by the term's columns, keeps none of the term's columns.

dimension.definition: The number of columns of the term, which is the number of random effects for each level.

informative_levels.definition: The number of levels in which the term's columns, restricted to the level's rows, have rank equal to dimension by the sequential rule.

levels.definition: The number of levels of the term's grouping factor in the design sample.

entries.summary: Compares the number of levels of a grouping factor with the number of random effects that a term estimates for each level. When the term's columns also appear in the fixed part, J levels support a covariance matrix of rank at most J - 1, and at most J otherwise, so a term whose dimension exceeds this bound gives a singular fit whatever the data, and a fit reported as non-singular then suggests that the optimiser stopped early. Levels in which the term's columns do not all vary inform the covariance only in part, so few informative levels make a singular fit likely.
entries.title: Levels against the dimension of a random term

entries.applies_when: The columns of the pattern, as pattern_terms defines it, are the intercept and columns coded from factors, so that its rows take finitely many patterns.

rules.condition: replicated_cells is 0, the family class is gaussian or other, and correlated or intercept_alone is true.
replicated_cells is 0 and the family class is bernoulli.
replicated_cells is 0 and the family class is gaussian or other.

bernoulli.template: Each combination of a level of '{factor}' and a cell of {terms} has one row, so '{term}' acts as an observation-level effect, whose variance ungrouped binary data do not identify.

coding_dependent.template: Each combination of a level of '{factor}' and a cell of {terms} has one row. With uncorrelated random effects, '{term}' is identified only through the restriction that the coding imposes, if at all, and the result changes with the coding. identifiability.gram_rank decides whether the coding chosen identifies it.

confounded.template: Each combination of a level of '{factor}' and a cell of '{term}' has one row, so the random effects of '{term}' are confounded with the residual and not identified.

overdispersion.template: Each combination of a level of '{factor}' and a cell of {terms} has one row, so '{term}' acts as an observation-level effect, which models overdispersion in this family.

replicated.fallback: Some combinations of a level of '{factor}' and a cell of {terms} have two or more rows.
replicated.template: Combinations of a level of '{factor}' and a cell of {terms} that have two or more rows: {replicated} of {cells}.

references.citation: Review catalogue (docs/design/evidence/review-catalogue.md), L1-05 and L7-14, with the verifiers' corrections on coding and on families.
Harrison, X. A. (2014). Using observation-level random effects to model overdispersion in count data in ecology and evolution. PeerJ, 2, e616.
Harrison, X. A. (2015). A comparison of observation-level random effect and Beta-Binomial models for modelling overdispersion in Binomial data in ecology & evolution. PeerJ, 3, e1114.

The R-sig-mixed-models thread 'reference on unidentifiability of observation-level variance in Bernoulli variables?' (2011) states that the observation-level variance of ungrouped Bernoulli data is not identifiable, which the message for the bernoulli family class states.

remedies.description: Remove the term, whose variance the residual already carries, or reduce it to the components that replicated cells identify.

cells.definition: The number of distinct combinations of a level of the term's grouping factor and a pattern of the columns of the pattern terms in the design sample, two rows having the same pattern when all these columns are equal.

columns.definition: The number of columns of the term.

correlated.definition: Whether the term has two or more columns and estimates their correlations.

intercept_alone.definition: Whether the term's one column is the intercept and pattern_terms holds the term alone.

pattern_terms.definition: The random terms whose columns form the pattern of the cells: the term itself when it is correlated, and otherwise every random term of the same grouping factor that has one column, in IR order, which are the terms that model uncorrelated effects of the factor.

replicated_cells.definition: The number of those combinations that hold at least two rows. The combinations with one row, cells minus replicated_cells, each hold one row, and both counts resolve over the combinations, so that a combination with one member makes them person counts.

entries.summary: For a random term whose columns come from factors, checks whether any combination of a level of its grouping factor and a cell of its columns holds more than one row. With one row per combination, as with a subject-by-item intercept in a Latin-square design or one observation per subject and condition, a Gaussian model cannot separate a random intercept or a correlated block from the residual. Uncorrelated terms of one factor, such as those that '||' writes, are judged together, and with one row per combination they are identified only through the restriction their coding imposes, if at all, which identifiability.gram_rank decides. For Bernoulli outcomes the term acts as an observation-level effect, whose variance ungrouped binary data do not identify, whereas for binomial outcomes with trials and counts it is an overdispersion term (Harrison, 2014, 2015).
entries.title: Random effects confounded with the residual

availability.condition: The declaration gives no observation key, or the key or one of its columns is inferred (registry.md, Terms).

conflicting.fallback: Some values of the observation key {key} are shared by rows that differ in other columns. Each row must have its own key value.
conflicting.template: Values of the observation key {key} shared by rows that differ in other columns: {conflicting}. Values shared only by identical rows: {identical}. Rows with a shared value: {rows}. Each row must have its own key value.

double_import.fallback: Some values of the observation key {key} are shared by identical rows, which suggests rows imported twice. Remove the copies at the source.
double_import.template: Values of the observation key {key} shared by identical rows: {identical}, with {rows} in all, which suggests rows imported twice. Remove the copies at the source.

missing_key.fallback: Some rows have a missing value in the observation key {key}.
missing_key.template: Rows with a missing value in the observation key {key}: {missing}.

unique.template: Every row has its own value of the observation key {key}.

references.citation: Review catalogue (docs/design/evidence/review-catalogue.md), L1-15 and L7-19.

remedies.description: Correct the duplicated or missing key values at the source. The packages never remove rows automatically.

conflicting_keys.definition: The number of duplicated key values whose rows differ in a compared column, compared by value with missing values equal to each other. The compared columns are those that the IR reads and those that the declaration gives a role, other than the response, its trials column and the columns that the declaration gives the role outcome or outcome_derived.

duplicate_rows.definition: The number of rows without a missing key value whose key value occurs in another such row.

duplicated_keys.definition: The number of distinct values of the key, among rows without a missing key value, that occur in two or more rows. Key values are compared by value (registry.md, Terms), as the table reader compares keys.

identical_keys.definition: duplicated_keys minus conflicting_keys. Either of the two is suppressed with the other, so that the written duplicated_keys cannot give back a suppressed one.

key_columns.definition: The columns of the declared observation key, in the declared order.

missing_key_rows.definition: The number of rows with a missing value in a key column.

rows.definition: The number of rows of the table.

entries.summary: Checks that every row of the table has its own value of the declared observation key. Identical rows are legitimate in trial-level data without a trial index, so duplicates are judged against the key and never against whole rows, and rows are never removed automatically. A key value shared by rows that differ elsewhere is an error in the data, and one shared by identical rows suggests rows imported twice. The check runs on the whole table, before rows with missing values are removed, and compares the columns it may read at T0, which exclude the outcome.
entries.title: Duplicates of the declared observation key

entries.applies_when: The column holds labels: a grouping column, a categorical predictor of the IR, a column of the declared observation key, the column of an entry of the assignment block or a column that the declaration gives the role assigned. The outcome is not read.

distinct.template: No two labels in '{column}' differ only in their Unicode form.

merged.fallback: In '{column}', distinct spellings that differ only in their Unicode form are treated as one label each.
merged.template: In '{column}', {spellings} that differ only in their Unicode form are treated as {labels}.

references.citation: conventions.md, Text and Unicode, and 02-decisions.md, cross-cutting conventions

remedies.description: Normalise the labels to NFC in the data source, so that other software reading the data treats them as the analysis does.

labels.definition: The number of distinct NFC forms that those strings share.

spellings.definition: The number of distinct strings of the column in the table that share their NFC form with another distinct string of the column. A string that is not normalisable stands for itself (conventions.md, NFC).

entries.summary: Labels are compared after NFC normalisation (conventions.md, Text and Unicode), so distinct spellings that are canonically equivalent, such as a precomposed and a decomposed accented letter, count as one label. The check reports each column in which such spellings occur, so that the merge is visible rather than silent. It compares no case and no white space.

entries.applies_when: The declared measurement of the outcome is bounded_score, and the outcome is a numeric column.

availability.condition: The declaration gives no measurement level for the outcome.
The declared measurement of the outcome is bounded_score, and the declaration gives no bounds for it, as when they are inferred.

rules.condition: floor_share exceeds floor or ceiling_share exceeds ceiling.

at_bounds.fallback: More than {threshold} of the rows are at a bound of the score. Consider a binomial or beta-binomial model when the maximum is a number of items, or an item-level model when item responses exist, and report any interaction on both scales.
at_bounds.template: Of the rows, {floor_share} are at the lowest possible score and {ceiling_share} at the highest, more than {threshold} at a bound. Consider a binomial or beta-binomial model when the maximum is a number of items, or an item-level model when item responses exist, and report any interaction on both scales.

within_bounds.fallback: No more than {threshold} of the rows are at either bound of the score.
within_bounds.template: Of the rows, {floor_share} are at the lowest possible score and {ceiling_share} at the highest, no more than {threshold} at either bound.

references.citation: Review catalogue (docs/design/evidence/review-catalogue.md), L3-12 and L7-20.

remedies.description: Model a sum of item scores as binomial or beta-binomial with the maximum as trials, or fit an item-level model when item responses exist.
Report an interaction on both the observed and a latent scale, with a note that it may depend on the scale.

at_ceiling.definition: The number of rows whose value of the outcome column equals the double nearest to the upper declared bound.

at_floor.definition: The number of rows whose value of the outcome column, as the table reader returns it and before any transform of the formula, equals the double nearest to the lower declared bound. Values outside the bounds count at neither bound.

rows.definition: The number of rows of the analysis sample.

entries.summary: For a score with declared bounds, reports the share of rows of the analysis sample at the lowest and at the highest possible value. A mass at a bound compresses variance, makes residuals heteroscedastic and turns additive effects on a latent scale into interactions on the observed scale. The 15% cut-off is a psychometric reporting convention for floor and ceiling effects, and the check reports it without choosing a model. Shares within design cells relate the outcome to predictors and belong to T2.

ceiling.rationale: More than 15% of respondents at the highest possible score is a common criterion for a ceiling effect in the validation of health status questionnaires, where each respondent gives one score. Applying it to the rows of an analysis sample, which can hold several rows of one person, is this project's extension.

sources.citation: Terwee, C. B., Bot, S. D. M., de Boer, M. R., van der Windt, D. A. W. M., Knol, D. L., Dekker, J., Bouter, L. M., & de Vet, H. C. W. (2007). Quality criteria were proposed for measurement properties of health status questionnaires. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 60(1), 34-42.

floor.rationale: More than 15% of respondents at the lowest possible score is a common criterion for a floor effect in the validation of health status questionnaires, where each respondent gives one score. Applying it to the rows of an analysis sample, which can hold several rows of one person, is this project's extension.

many.fallback: The outcome is constant within at least a quarter of the levels of '{factor}' that have two or more rows. For a binary outcome, this can push the standard deviation of the random intercept towards very large values, and by-'{factor}' slopes rest on the other levels.
many.template: The outcome is constant within {constant} of the {levels} of '{factor}' with two or more rows ({share}). For a binary outcome, this can push the standard deviation of the random intercept towards very large values, and by-'{factor}' slopes rest on the other levels.

no_levels.template: No level of '{factor}' has two or more rows, so variation within levels cannot be assessed.

none_constant.template: The outcome varies within every level of '{factor}' that has two or more rows.

some.fallback: The outcome is constant within some of the levels of '{factor}' that have two or more rows.
some.template: The outcome is constant within {constant} of the {levels} of '{factor}' with two or more rows.

remedies.description: Report the share of constant levels with the variance estimates, and treat a very large standard deviation of the random intercept as a consequence of these levels.
Where the design allows, model binary rows as binomial counts per cell with their trials, which gives the same estimates and comparable dispersion statistics.

constant_levels.definition: The number of those levels within which the response vector of ir.md (Response, offsets and weights) takes one value, so that for a binary outcome with a declared event level all the other categories count as one. A categorical outcome without a response vector, such as an ordinal item, is constant in a level when its labels, compared after NFC, take one value there. For the binomial family class, a level is constant when all its rows have no events or all have as many events as trials.

constant_share.definition: constant_levels divided by multi_row_levels, absent when multi_row_levels is 0.

multi_row_levels.definition: The number of levels of the factor with at least two rows in the analysis sample. A level with one row is not counted, whatever its number of trials.

entries.summary: Counts the levels of a grouping factor within which the outcome does not vary. For a binary outcome, as with participants at 100% accuracy, such levels contribute almost nothing to their own random slopes, and many of them can push the standard deviation of the random intercept towards very large values. For other outcomes, constant levels point to floor or ceiling effects or to errors in the data. The check reads the outcome by grouping factor only.

any.rationale: One constant level is reported so that its effect on the slopes can be judged.

many.rationale: A quarter of the levels without variation is taken as many, the point at which the variance estimates rest largely on the other levels. The cut-off is a convention, to be calibrated in the GLMM studies V8 to V10.

rules.condition: The finding is for the model as a whole.

events.fallback: The statistics give the events and non-events of the outcome and the minority events in the levels of '{factor}' as far as they can be shown.
events.template: The outcome has {events} and {non_events}, or {per_column} minority events per fixed-effects column. One of the two classes is absent in {without} of the {levels} of '{factor}', counting the levels with one row, and the median level has {median}.

events_model.fallback: The statistics give the events and non-events of the outcome as far as they can be shown.
events_model.template: The outcome has {events} and {non_events}, or {per_column} minority events per fixed-effects column.

references.citation: Review catalogue (docs/design/evidence/review-catalogue.md), L3-20 and L3-21.

events.definition: The number of events in the analysis sample: rows whose value of the response vector of ir.md (Response, offsets and weights) is 1 for the bernoulli family class, and the sum of the event counts for the binomial family class.

events_per_column.definition: The smaller of events and non-events divided by the statistic kept of design.rank_deficiency, the number of fixed-effects columns that the sequential rule keeps on the design sample, so that the check reads no predictor. It is absent when kept is 0. With kept, which is written, it gives back the minority count, so it is suppressed with events and non_events.

levels.definition: The number of levels of the factor in the analysis sample, absent for a finding for the model as a whole.

levels_without_minority.definition: The number of levels in which the smaller of the level's events and non-events is 0, levels of one row included, absent for a finding for the model as a whole.

median_minority.definition: The level minority count at position ceil(J/2) when the smaller of each level's events and non-events are sorted in increasing order, with J the number of levels, which is the quantile 0.5 of the J level minority counts. It is absent for a finding for the model as a whole.

non_events.definition: The number of rows, or of trials for the binomial family class, minus events. events and non_events add up to the rows, or the trials, so either is suppressed with the other.

entries.summary: For binary and binomial outcomes, the information about effects grows with the number of events in the minority class rather than with the number of rows. The check reports the events and non-events in the analysis sample, the minority count in each level of a grouping factor and the minority events per fixed-effects column, as an index without a cut-off. It reads the outcome by grouping factor only. A model without grouping factors yields one finding for the model as a whole, with the counts of the analysis sample.

The family class is bernoulli, the outcome takes values other than 0 and 1, as numbers or logical values, in the analysis sample, and the IR gives the response no event level (registry.md, Terms).

complete.fallback: The fixed effects separate the events from the non-events completely, so the estimates of some coefficients diverge and their Wald statistics are unreliable.
complete.template: The fixed effects separate the events from the non-events completely, through {columns}, so the estimates of these coefficients diverge and their Wald statistics are unreliable.

no_solution.template: The solver gave no verified optimum of the linear programs, so separation could not be assessed.

none.template: The fixed effects do not separate the events from the non-events.

one_class.template: The analysis sample holds only events or only non-events, so separation cannot be assessed.

quasi.fallback: The fixed effects separate the events from the non-events quasi-completely, so the estimates of some coefficients diverge and their Wald statistics are unreliable.
quasi.template: The fixed effects separate the events from the non-events quasi-completely, through {columns}, so the estimates of these coefficients diverge and their Wald statistics are unreliable.

bound_tolerance.definition: The difference within which the coefficient bounds from the two packages agree, and, relative to the larger of 1 and the two values, the optimum and the margin (02-decisions.md, Q2, and conventions.md, Comparison across languages).

sources.citation: 02-decisions.md, Q2

feasibility_tolerance.definition: The amount by which a value u of a returned solution may fall below 0 and the solution still count as verified.

sources.citation: Set by this project for registry 0.1.0. In a review of registry 0.1.0, lpSolve with scale = 0 returned solutions whose smallest u lay near -1.3e-8 on data of 200 rows, and HiGHS with its default tolerance of 1e-7 accepted violations up to that tolerance, which made data that overlap in exact arithmetic quasi-separated. On 2,000 rows that only b = 0 separates in exact arithmetic, with one event and one non-event a gap g apart around 0.5, lpSolve returned an optimum near 500 with smallest u = -g for g = 1e-8 and 1e-9, where HiGHS at 1e-9 returned b = 0, so a verified solution with some u below minus residue_tolerance makes the finding near_threshold.

involvement_tolerance.definition: The absolute value above which a bound of a coefficient over the optimal face involves its column in the separation. It is ten times separation_tolerance, so that bounds that the two packages compare within bound_tolerance name the same columns, and a finding is near_threshold when a bound lies within the proximity factor of it.

sources.citation: Set by this project for registry 0.1.0.

residue_tolerance.definition: The amount by which a value u of a verified solution may fall below 0 without making the finding near_threshold. A value of u computed in double arithmetic from a returned b can fall a little below 0 where its exact value is 0, which says nothing about the data, whereas a violation through which a solver reaches a large optimum on data that no b other than 0 separates is as large as the gap in the data, such as the values -1e-8 and -1e-9 of the review of feasibility_tolerance. Data whose gap on the scaled columns is below this value can therefore be reported as separated with the status clear.

sources.citation: Set by this project for registry 0.1.0. In M2b-2, lpSolve with scale = 0 and the variables c_j = b_j + 1 returned, on the audit-corpus cases audits-outcome-028, 029 and 031, solutions whose smallest u lay between -3.4e-13 and 0 where the exact value is 0, and on overlapping data of 40 to 2,000 rows smallest values of u down to -5e-12. Through the dual, it left smallest values of u down to -2.6e-13 on the programs of 84 generated tables of 200 to 160,000 observations, each less than half of this parameter in absolute value.

separation_tolerance.definition: The value above which the verified margin or optimum, computed on columns scaled to a largest absolute value of 1, indicates separation, so that complete means separation with a margin above it on the scaled columns. A finding is near_threshold when the margin or the optimum lies within the proximity factor of it (registry.md, Parameters).

sources.citation: Set by this project for registry 0.1.0, well above the feasibility tolerances of lpSolve, 1e-10 by default, and of HiGHS as the check sets them, 1e-9.

references.citation: Albert, A., & Anderson, J. A. (1984). On the existence of maximum likelihood estimates in logistic regression models. Biometrika, 71(1), 1-10.

Albert and Anderson (1984) prove the result for logistic regression. In a model with random effects, the likelihood conditional on any value of the random effects increases monotonically along a separating direction of the fixed effects, and so does its integral over the random effects, so the estimates of the fixed effects diverge there too.
Konis, K. (2007). Linear programming algorithms for detecting separated data in binary logistic regression models [Doctoral thesis, University of Oxford]. Oxford University Research Archive.

remedies.description: Merge sparse levels or remove the interaction that creates the separation, if this was declared as a contingency before the outcome was seen.
Use penalised or Bayesian estimation with weakly informative priors on the fixed effects, and report likelihood-ratio tests or profile intervals for the affected terms rather than Wald tests.

both_classes.definition: Whether events and non_events are both above 0.

bounds.definition: When verdict is quasi or complete, for each kept column in column order, the smallest and the largest value of b_j over the optimal face of the first program, the set of b that meets its constraints with a sum of s x'b of at least optimum minus separation_tolerance, each found by a linear program solved and verified as above, as the pairs (smallest, largest) laid out in one list. The programs run in column order, the smallest before the largest, and stop at the first that has no verified solution, so that the programs after it are not solved and cannot make the finding near_threshold. Both packages compare these values within bound_tolerance. It is absent otherwise, or when one of these programs has no verified solution.

columns.definition: The number of fixed-effects columns of the analysis sample that the sequential rule keeps, the columns of the linear programs. Beside the kept columns of the design sample, it would show that the rows without an outcome emptied a cell of the predictors.

columns_involved.definition: The kept columns whose largest value in bounds is above involvement_tolerance or whose smallest value is below minus involvement_tolerance, in column order, absent when bounds is absent.

events.definition: The number of observations, as verdict defines them, with s = 1: the rows with an event, and for the binomial family class the rows with k above 0.

margin.definition: v2, the smaller of 1 and the smallest u for the verified solution of the second program, which is its optimal t and so does not depend on which optimal solution the solver returns when t reaches its bound of 1. It is absent when the second program has no verified solution or is not solved, and it is compared as optimum is.

non_events.definition: The number of observations with s = -1: the rows without an event, and for the binomial family class the rows with k below n.

optimum.definition: v1, the sum over observations of u for the verified solution of the first program, summed exactly and rounded once, as ir.md (Centring) sums values. It is absent when the first program has no verified solution or is not solved. The two packages compare it within bound_tolerance relative to the larger of 1 and the two values (conventions.md, Comparison across languages).

verdict.definition: Let X be the fixed-effects columns of the analysis sample that the sequential rule keeps, each divided by its largest absolute value. Each row gives one observation with sign s = 1 when it is an event and s = -1 otherwise. For the binomial family class, a row with k events of n trials gives an observation with s = 1 when k is above 0 and one with s = -1 when k is below n. The first linear program maximises the sum over observations of s x'b subject to s x'b >= 0 for every observation and -1 <= b_j <= 1 for every coefficient. The second maximises t subject to s x'b >= t for every observation, the same bounds on b and t <= 1. A program of bounds below adds g'b >= f, with g the sum over observations of s x and f a floor, to the constraints of the first, and maximises b_j or -b_j. In R, each program is solved with lpSolve::lp() with scale = 0, since the columns are already scaled, through its dual. For a program that maximises c'b, or t for the second, the dual minimises the sum over coefficients of w+_j + w-_j, minus f r for a program of bounds and plus z for the second, over y_i for each observation, w+_j, w-_j, r and z, all at least 0, subject to w+_j - w-_j - (sum over observations of y_i s x_ij) - r g_j = c_j for each coefficient, with c = 0 for the second, and, for the second, the sum of the y_i plus z = 1. b is the vector of the dual values of the constraints of the coefficients, which lp() returns with compute.sens = 1. The dual has one constraint for each coefficient, and one more for the second program, whatever the number of observations. When lp() reports no optimum for the dual, or its b is not verified, the program itself is solved, with b_j = b+_j - b-_j and 0 <= b+_j, b-_j <= 1 as the solver's variables, the upper bounds written as constraints. It has one constraint for each observation, and its time grows about as the power 1.7 of their number. In Python, each program is solved through the same dual with scipy.optimize.linprog() with method 'highs-ds' and the options primal_feasibility_tolerance and dual_feasibility_tolerance set to 1e-9, b being the first p elements of res.eqlin.marginals, and the program itself with the same options when the dual has no verified solution. A solution is verified when the solver reports an optimum and every u = s x'b, computed from the returned b in double arithmetic, is at least minus feasibility_tolerance. A verified solution with some u below minus residue_tolerance meets the constraints only within the feasibility tolerance, and a solver can reach a large optimum through such a violation on data that no b other than 0 separates in exact arithmetic, so the finding is then near_threshold, whichever program it solves. Values of u between minus residue_tolerance and 0 leave the finding clear. They are the rounding residues of the solver's arithmetic where the exact value is 0, or the violation that data whose events and non-events overlap by less than about residue_tolerance on the scaled columns allow, which the check then reports as separated. Conversely, on separated data whose margin on the scaled columns lies below the solvers' tolerances, as when an outlier makes the other values of its column small after scaling, one solver can return b = 0 and the verdict none, clear, where the other returns quasi through a solution that is near_threshold, as conventions.md (Comparison across languages) allows. Were that solution to meet the constraints within residue_tolerance, both findings would be clear and their verdicts would differ, which these tolerances do not exclude. The verdict is complete when the verified margin of the second program is above separation_tolerance, quasi otherwise when the verified optimum of the first is above separation_tolerance, and none otherwise. When both_classes is false, the programs are not solved, and verdict, optimum, margin, bounds and columns_involved are absent. The verdict is also absent when either program has no verified solution.

entries.summary: Tests by linear programming whether the fixed-effects columns separate the events from the non-events completely or quasi-completely, in which case the maximum-likelihood estimates of the fixed effects diverge (Albert & Anderson, 1984), with random effects as without them. An all-0 or all-1 cell is neither necessary nor sufficient for separation, which depends only on the column space of the fixed effects, so the verdict does not change with the coding. The programs run in an external solver, lpSolve in R and HiGHS through scipy in Python, with the settings stated below. Each solution is verified in double arithmetic before the verdict is decided, so that both packages decide on the same verified quantities, and the range of each coefficient over the optimal face is reported, because different solvers can return different optimal vertices. The check relates the outcome to the predictors, so Stream B runs it only in its exploratory mode (02-decisions.md, Q2 and Q3).

The R-sig-mixed-models thread 'reference on unidentifiability of observation-level variance in Bernoulli variables?' (2011) states that the observation-level variance of ungrouped Bernoulli data is not identifiable and refers to McCullagh and Nelder, Generalized linear models, 2nd edition, section 4.5, which this project has not read. The message states no more than the thread. effective_size.definition: The effective level size n0 = (N - S/N)/(J - 1), where S is the sum of the squared level sizes, for which the expected between-level mean square of a one-way layout is the residual variance plus n0 times the variance of the factor. S is summed in integer arithmetic, and S/N, the difference and the quotient are each computed in double arithmetic, so that it is 'NaN' when J is 1, the quotient being 0/0. With N and J, it gives back the level sizes of a factor with few levels, and with J it gives back N, since S is an integer, so it is suppressed with the lower quartile and with N.

intercept.definition: Whether a random term of the factor has an intercept.

largest.definition: The largest number of rows in a level, the quantile 1.

levels.definition: The number of levels of the factor in the design sample, J.

lower_quartile.definition: The level size at position ceil(J/4) when the level sizes are sorted in increasing order and counted from 1, which is the quantile 0.25 of the J level sizes by the inverse of their empirical distribution function.

median.definition: The level size at position ceil(J/2) in the same order, the quantile 0.5.

rows.definition: The number of rows of the design sample, N.

singletons.definition: The number of levels with one row. Each holds one row, so the count is also a count of rows, and its class is person whatever the factor.

A random intercept of a factor with one row per level duplicates the residual in a Gaussian model, whereas for counts and binomial outcomes with trials it is an observation-level random effect, a standard term for overdispersion (Harrison, 2014, 2015).

The check looks in both directions, each with one column of the pair as the labels column and the other as the context column, and computes the statistics below in each. It reports the only direction that has candidate attributes. When both have them, it reports the direction whose changing_labels is above 0 when that of the other is 0, since the other direction then has an attribute that stays constant across its shared labels, as an attribute of its units does, so that the change in the reported direction cannot come from the other column repeating its labels. Otherwise, and when neither direction has candidate attributes, it reports the direction whose labels column is the first column.

shared_labels.definition: The number of labels of the labels column that occur with more than one label of the context column in the same rows, which structure.label_incidence counts as first_in_several or second_in_several, so that it is suppressed with them.

tied.definition: Whether both directions have candidate attributes and changing_labels above 0, so that every candidate attribute changes across the shared labels of both columns and the attributes cannot show which of the two columns repeats its labels, since a column that repeats its labels makes the attributes of its units change in both directions.

entries.summary: When labels of one grouping column occur with several labels of another and the declaration states no relation between the two units, the check reports outcome-free evidence on whether a repeated label denotes one unit or several: whether attributes that are fixed for a unit keep their value across the levels of the other column. In mlmRev's Exam data, 269 of 322 shared student labels change sex across schools, whereas in a crossed psycholinguistic dataset none of 600 items changes its frequency or length (02-decisions.md, Q4). An attribute can show which column repeats its labels only when another attribute stays constant across the shared labels of the other column: in Exam, sex also changes within 35 of the 65 schools, so sex alone leaves the direction open, whereas the school attribute schgend, constant within every school, points to the student labels. The evidence informs a declaration and never decides the coding.

relation.definition: The first of these values whose condition holds, tested in the order listed: identical when first_in_several and second_in_several are both 0, first_nested_in_second when first_in_several is 0, second_nested_in_first when second_in_several is 0, crossed when combinations equals levels_first multiplied by levels_second, and partially_crossed otherwise. So neither first_in_several nor second_in_several is 0 for crossed and partially_crossed.

second_in_several.definition: The number of labels of the second column that occur with more than one label of the first.

entries.summary: Classifies how the labels of two grouping columns occur together in the design sample: as identical partitions, as one column nested in the other, fully crossed or partially crossed. It then compares the observed relation, and the way the IR combines the two columns into grouping factors, with the relation, ID scope and membership that the declaration states for the units the columns label. Labels that repeat under several outer units cannot show whether they denote one unit or several (02-decisions.md, Q4), so the check never recodes a column.
entries.title: Label incidence between grouping columns

entries.applies_when: The sequential rule, applied to the fixed-effects columns, keeps at least one column of the term.

rules.condition: status is between, slope_requested is true and varying_levels is 0, so that the term is exactly constant within every level.
status is between and slope_requested is true, the term being constant within the levels only with the tolerance of agreement.
status is partially_within and slope_requested is true.

between_slope.template: As inferred from the data, '{term}' does not vary within the levels of '{factor}', so a by-'{factor}' slope for it can only describe how the variance between levels changes with '{term}'. Its variance is not a slope variance and may not be identified. Remove the slope, or keep it only as a model of between-level variance.

no_levels.template: No level of '{factor}' has two or more rows, so whether '{term}' varies within its levels cannot be assessed.

partial_slope.fallback: As inferred from the data, '{term}' varies within only some of the levels of '{factor}' that have two or more rows, so its by-'{factor}' slope rests on those levels alone.
partial_slope.template: As inferred from the data, '{term}' varies within {varying} of the {levels} of '{factor}' with two or more rows, and in all its kept columns within {informative}, so its by-'{factor}' slope rests on those levels alone.

status.fallback: As inferred from the data, '{term}' is {status} with respect to '{factor}'.
status.template: As inferred from the data, '{term}' is {status} with respect to '{factor}': it varies within {varying} of its {levels} with two or more rows.

agreement.definition: The share of the rows of the levels with at least two rows that must have the most frequent pattern of their level for the factor to count as constant in the term (registry.md, Terms).

sources.citation: 02-decisions.md, Q4. A rule that required 99% agreement within clusters, pooled over the rows of all clusters, recovered the school level in 99.3 to 100% of 2,000 replicates with up to 0.5% of rows miscoded (evidence/decisions/E-verify/scripts/exp2_tolerant.py, rule R2). The same share applied to each cluster separately behaves as the exact rule R1 for clusters of fewer than 100 rows.

references.citation: Review catalogue (docs/design/evidence/review-catalogue.md), L1-03, with the verifier's correction on coding and on the number of distinct values.

remedies.description: Remove the by-factor slope of a term that does not vary within the factor's levels, and model differences in variance between levels explicitly if they matter.

Separate the within-level and between-level parts of a numeric predictor: add its level means over the design sample and the deviations from them as columns declared with derived_from, and use both as predictors.

icc.definition: For a term with one kept column whose variables are all numeric, the ANOVA intraclass correlation of the column across the levels, (MSB - MSW) / (MSB + (n0 - 1) MSW), with MSB = SSB/(J - 1), MSW = SSW/(N - J), SSB the sum over levels of the level size times the squared difference between the level mean and the overall mean, SSW the sum of squared differences from the level means and n0 as structure.cluster_sizes defines it. The column is first divided by its largest absolute value, which changes neither icc nor within_share, so that its squares neither overflow nor underflow, and the overall and level means of the scaled column are summed exactly and divided once, as ir.md (Centring) computes means. It is absent for other terms and when the column is constant over the design sample, compared by value, and 'NaN' when J is 1, when N equals J or when the denominator is 0, so that its absence depends on no count of levels or rows (privacy.md, Steps). With within_share and the rows of the design sample, it gives back J and the sum of the squared level sizes, which are integers, so a shareable document never writes it.

informative_levels.definition: The number of levels counted in varying_levels in which the rank by the sequential rule of the term's kept columns, restricted to the level's rows, after the level's first row is subtracted from every row, equals the number of the term's kept columns.

multi_row_levels.definition: The number of levels of the factor with at least two rows in the design sample.

slope_requested.definition: Whether a random term of the IR with this grouping factor has a term whose set of variables equals that of this fixed term, as estimands are matched with terms (declarations.md, estimands).

status.definition: between when the factor is constant in the term's kept columns with the parameter agreement, pooled over its levels with at least two rows (registry.md, Terms), so that a few miscoded rows do not make the term vary, within otherwise when varying_levels equals multi_row_levels, and partially_within otherwise. It is absent when multi_row_levels is 0.

varying_levels.definition: The number of levels with at least two rows in which the term varies: levels whose rows do not all have the same pattern of the term's kept columns, the columns of the term that the sequential rule keeps when it is applied to the fixed-effects columns. Patterns are compared by value (registry.md, Terms).

within_share.definition: For the same terms, SSW / (SSB + SSW), the share of the column's variation that lies within levels, with SSB and SSW those of icc, computed from the scaled column. It is absent when the column is constant over the design sample, when SSB + SSW is 0 or for other terms.

entries.summary: For each fixed term other than the intercept and each grouping factor, reports whether the term varies within the levels of the factor, how many levels inform a slope for it and, for a single numeric column, its intraclass correlation. Whether a term varies within a level is inferred with the tolerance of 02-decisions.md (Q4), so that a few miscoded rows do not turn a term that is constant within levels into one that varies, and the messages say that the status was inferred from the data. A by-factor slope for a term that does not vary within any level only describes how the variance between levels changes with the term. Whether such a variance is identified depends on the coding and on the number of distinct values, and it is never a slope variance.
